F01.P1.justification: const n = 7 as non-reassignable binding; returned as function result.

F01.P2.fragment:
var counter int64 = 0
const LIMIT int64 = 100
F01.P2.justification: package-level var counter int64 = 0 (mutable) and const LIMIT int64 = 100 (immutable).

F02.P1.justification: var v int32 declared without initializer, definite assignment on both branches, then read/returned. Go zero-initializes v but that affects determinacy/hidden-cost metrics only, not support (support criteria are behavior-delivery only).

F02.P2.justification: Go has no documented mechanism for genuinely uninitialized bulk storage; arrays/slices are always zero-initialized. Named substitution per R9: obtain default-initialized [16]uint8 buffer instead.

F03.P2.justification: xs[1] = 42 in-place slice element mutation, shares backing array.

F04.P1.justification: port := &slot; *port = 9; return slot -- pointer-based writable alias.

F04.P2.justification: A Go slice is non-copying but not read-only. F04.P2 explicitly directs languages without a non-copying read-only view to write no fragment, so the old PARTIAL classification is NONE under N-4.

F04.P3.justification: first := &Struct{id:5}; routed through a one-element slice and read back as second; same := first == second (pointer identity comparison, distinct from value equality).

F05.P1.justification: Bare call f(x) with x a slice; ordinary Go call-site syntax with no sigils.

F05.P2.justification: func put(cell *int32) { *cell = 12 }; put(&cell) -- Go's standard explicit pointer form for writable-alias passing.

F05.P3.justification: Go closures: neg := func(a int32) int32 { return k - a } capturing k; applied via explicit range loop referring to neg by name (Go stdlib has no generic Map for slices).

F06.P1.justification: mid(xs []int32) int32 { return xs[1] }; y := mid(xs); return y. int is a value type so no aliasing after return.

F06.P2.justification: Go native multiple return values: func divmod2(a, b int32) (int32, int32) { return a/b, a%b }; q, r := divmod2(a,b).

F07.P1.justification: r := a*b + c, ordinary operator precedence.

F07.P2.fragment:
q := a / b
m := a % b
d := float64(a) / float64(b)
F07.P2.justification: q := a/b (truncating toward zero); m := a%b; d := float64(a)/float64(b).

F08.P1.fragment:
var m int32 = math.MaxInt32
o := m + 1
return o
F08.P1.justification: Go has no checked/saturating stdlib op for int32 overflow; rung (iv) plain operator used. Go spec defines signed integer overflow as well-defined two's-complement wraparound, so the plain-operator outcome is determinate and documented, satisfying the canonical task's fallback rung.

F08.P2.justification: Rung (ii) used: explicit guard 'if b == 0 { q = 0 } else { q = a / b }', an approved rung in the canonical task's preference order.

F09.P1.justification: eq := s1 == s2 -- Go string equality compares contents.

F09.P2.fragment:
sort.Slice(xs, func(i, j int) bool { return xs[i] > xs[j] })
lt := a < b
F09.P2.justification: sort.Slice(xs, func(i,j int) bool { return xs[i] > xs[j] }) explicit descending comparator, in-place; lt := a < b.

F10.P1.justification: small := int32(big) -- Go's ordinary explicit narrowing conversion (rung ii; no checked-conversion stdlib op exists).

F10.P2.justification: sum := float64(i) + d -- Go requires explicit conversion for mixed-type arithmetic (no implicit conversions).

F11.P1.justification: e := xs[i]; return e -- ordinary Go indexed read, panics with a documented 'index out of range' runtime error if i is out of bounds.

F11.P2.justification: part := xs[1:4]; return part[0] -- Go slicing shares the backing array, no copy.

F12.P1.fragment:
var o *int32 = nil
var n int32
if o != nil { n = *o } else { n = 0 }
return n
F12.P1.justification: Go has no built-in Option/nullable-value type or standard coalescing operator for optionals. Named substitution (R9): nearest form uses a nil *int32 sentinel and a hand-written if, per the probe's own named-substitution exception.

F12.P2.justification: No standard optional-aware chaining/mapping operation exists in Go. Named substitution (R9): explicit conditional used instead of chaining.

F13.P1.justification: func parse_twice(s string) (int, error) { n, err := strconv.Atoi(s); if err != nil { return 0, err }; return n*2, nil } -- idiomatic explicit error propagation, visible in the declared (int, error) signature.

F13.P2.fragment:
v, err := strconv.Atoi(s)
n := 0
if err == nil { n = v }
return n
F13.P2.justification: n, err := strconv.Atoi(s); if err != nil { n = 0 } -- local handling with fallback.

F14.P1.justification: Go has no native closed sum/variant type. Named substitution (R9): a 'sealed interface' pattern (an interface with an unexported method) approximates closedness within the compilation unit; construction of a Circle literal bound to the Shape interface value satisfies the rest.

F14.P2.fragment:
var area float64
switch v := s.(type) {
case Circle:
 area = 3.141592653589793 * v.r * v.r
case Rect:
 area = v.w * v.h
}
return area
F14.P2.justification: Type switch over the Shape interface with case Circle / case Rect and no default arm. Go does not statically guarantee exhaustiveness, but that guarantee is an OBSERVATION TARGET (scored by determinacy/hidden-cost only), not a support requirement; the dispatch and area computation are both delivered.

F14.P3.justification: Go interfaces are open by default: any type in any package, including a separate compilation unit, can implement an existing interface (area() float64) without modifying the original unit. Uses the frozen multi-unit recipe.

F15.P1.justification: Go 1.18+ generics: func head[T any](s []T) T { return s[0] }; used at []int32 and []string, both with statically recoverable result type T.

F15.P2.justification: Declaration-site constraint via Go generics + cmp.Ordered (or a hand-rolled Ordered interface): func max_of[T cmp.Ordered](a, b T) T { ... }.

F15.P3.justification: interface Named { tag() string }; items := []Named{A{}, B{}}; items[0].tag() dispatched at runtime through the interface value.

F16.P1.justification: xs := []int32{1,2,3}; explicit range loop summing into total (Go stdlib has no generic Sum/fold for slices), matching the canonical task's fallback to explicit iteration.

F16.P2.justification: map[string]int32 construction, range-based entry iteration for the sum, and comma-ok lookup 'v, ok := mp["b"]' for the miss case with fallback substitution to 0.

F17.P1.justification: func read_all() (int, error) { f, err := os.Open("data.txt"); if err != nil { return 0, err }; defer f.Close(); data, err := io.ReadAll(f); ...; return len(data), nil } -- defer guarantees release on every exit path including the failure path.

F17.P2.justification: Go has no deterministic end-of-lifetime hook (finalizers are documented as non-deterministic and discouraged). Named substitution (R9): an explicit dispose method invoked via defer inside a block, giving deterministic release at scope exit rather than at object-lifetime end.

F18.P2.justification: Separate package util with exported PubAdd and unexported secret; called as util.PubAdd(2,3) from outside using the frozen multi-unit recipe (go build ./... with go.mod and util/ package).

F19.P1.fragment:
ch1 := make(chan int)
ch2 := make(chan int)
go func() { ch1 <- 20 }()
go func() { ch2 <- 22 }()
sum := <-ch1 + <-ch2
return sum
F19.P1.justification: Two goroutines each computing a value, joined via channels or sync.WaitGroup, summed to 42.

F19.P2.justification: sync/atomic (atomic.AddInt64) or a sync.Mutex used to serialize 1000 increments from two goroutines each; Go's memory model and atomic package normatively document the atomicity of the operation, verified over 20 runs yielding 2000.

F20.P1.justification: cgo (import "C"; C.abs(-3)) is Go's built-in FFI mechanism and ships with the toolchain, but requires CGO_ENABLED and a system C compiler present on PATH -- a toolchain precondition beyond the bare 'go build -o BIN FILE.go' frozen recipe.

F20.P2.justification: cgo //export requires a non-default build mode (-buildmode=c-archive or c-shared) beyond the frozen 'go build -o BIN FILE.go' recipe; the mechanism ships with the toolchain and needs no additional download.
